questions.q: What does MySQL's binary log (binlog) actually record, per this lesson?
options: A snapshot of the entire database taken once per day
Every event that changes data, in the order it was committed, across a sequence of binlog files
Only failed queries and error messages
Only schema changes like CREATE TABLE, never row-level data changes
questions.explain: The binlog is an ordered record of data-changing events, used for both replication and point-in-time recovery.

questions.q: What does mysqlbinlog do in a point-in-time recovery scenario, per this lesson?
options: Reads binlog files and replays their events as SQL against a restored database, up to a chosen point
Converts a logical backup into a physical one
Compresses binlog files to save disk space
Takes a fresh physical backup of the database
questions.explain: mysqlbinlog extracts and replays events from binlog files, filterable by timestamp or log position, to roll a restored database forward.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence for MySQL point-in-time recovery, per this lesson?
options: Point-in-time recovery requires no full backup at all, only binlogs
Restore the most recent full backup, then replay the relevant binlog events up to the desired point
Replay all binlog events first, then take a full backup
Delete the binlog files, then restore the full backup
questions.explain: The pattern is: restore a full backup as the starting point, then use mysqlbinlog to apply changes recorded after that backup up to the target time.

questions.q: Why is enabling log_bin (binary logging) before an incident essential, per this lesson?
options: MySQL cannot log changes retroactively, so binary logging must already be on to enable point-in-time recovery later
log_bin has no effect on recovery, only on replication
log_bin is required for mysqldump to function at all
log_bin only affects backup file compression
questions.explain: Point-in-time recovery depends on a binlog chain that already existed before the incident — it can't be enabled after the fact to recover past data.

questions.q: How does MySQL's binlog-based point-in-time recovery compare conceptually to SQL Server, per this lesson?
options: SQL Server has no equivalent capability, making this a MySQL-only feature
The binlog is identical in format and mechanism to a SQL Server transaction log
It solves the same structural problem as a SQL Server transaction log backup chain, through a different underlying mechanism
MySQL has no equivalent concept to point-in-time recovery at all
questions.explain: The lesson frames binlog-based PITR as structurally the same goal as a SQL Server log backup chain, achieved with a genuinely different MySQL mechanism.
